title: Mus'ab the teacher
hook: Mus'ab ibn Umayr is sent to teach the Qur'an in Yathrib, and many believe

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first pledge of Aqaba. Your line was: a pledge of conduct. Did your one plain promise get tested? Day seven hundred sixty.

The twelve are heading home with a promise and a problem. They believe, but who will teach them? Who will recite the Qur'an to their families, lead their prayer, answer the questions that come up at dinner? So the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, sends someone with them. Not a clan elder. Mus'ab ibn Umayr, a Meccan who, tradition says, had left a comfortable life behind for this faith. Ibn Ishaq says that in Yathrib people came to call him simply the reciter. Today: Mus'ab the teacher.
screen: `WHO WILL TEACH THEM?` → `MUS'AB IS SENT.` → `THEY CALL HIM THE RECITER.`

segments.voice: Mus'ab stays with a man of Yathrib, As'ad ibn Zurara, and the two of them go out into the gardens and neighborhoods, reciting. Not everyone is pleased. Ibn Ishaq tells of one day when a clan leader, Usayd ibn Hudayr, comes striding toward them with his spear, angry. What have you come here for, to make fools of our weak ones? Leave us, if you value your life. And Mus'ab doesn't argue. He says, roughly: will you not sit down and listen? If you like what you hear, accept it. If you dislike it, we'll keep away from what you dislike. Usayd thinks that's fair. He plants his spear in the ground and sits. Mus'ab recites. And the story says that before Usayd had spoken a word, they could see the change in his face. He asks what a person does to enter this faith. Then Usayd goes and sends a greater leader, Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, who comes in just as angry, and the same thing happens: an invitation to sit, a recitation, a changed face. Ibn Ishaq says Sa'd then went back to his own clan and asked how they regarded him, and when they answered with respect, he told them he would not speak to them until they believed. And tradition says that by evening, his clan had. Here's what Mus'ab's teaching looks like. Sit down. Listen. You are free to say no. That's the whole method in the story. The teacher's job is to put the words in front of people, and step back.
screen: `A SPEAR AND A THREAT.` · `WILL YOU NOT SIT AND LISTEN?` · `IF YOU DISLIKE IT, WE STOP.` · `A CHANGED FACE.` · then, large: `THE FIRST TEACHER.`

segments.voice: The practice: teach one verse to someone. Sit, and breathe. Choose a short line you know, one you could say without a page in front of you. If you're Muslim, it might be a line from a short surah. In Pickthall's old translation, the hundred and twelfth surah opens: Say: He is Allah, the One! If you're not, it can be any line that matters to you. Now think of one person who might like to hear it: a child, a friend, a coworker who asked once. Picture saying it to them, the way Mus'ab did: here it is, take it or leave it. Then say the line once, quietly, to yourself. The bell holds the time.
Mus'ab the teacher. Sent with the believers of Yathrib, he recited the Qur'an to anyone who would sit, and left them free to say no. Today's word.
Your line: the first teacher. Today, pass on one line you love to one person, and let them do what they like with it. Day seven hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Muslims remember Mus'ab ibn Umayr as the teacher sent to Yathrib before the hijra, and his invitation to sit and listen is often retold when people talk about how to share the faith gently.

fork.reveal: he invited him to sit and listen, and promised to stop if he disliked it. Usayd planted his spear and sat.

original.note: Arabic: the reciter, the one who teaches the Qur'an aloud; Mus'ab's name in Yathrib.

trapdoor: what you thought: a missionary sent to convert a town.
what it means: a teacher who recited and then stepped back: sit, listen, you're free to say no.
what a scholar hears: Ibn Ishaq's account of Mus'ab ibn Umayr, called al-muqri' in Yathrib; the conversions of Usayd ibn Hudayr and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (Mus'ab sent with the men of the first Aqaba; called the reciter; stays with As'ad ibn Zurara; Usayd ibn Hudayr and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh accept Islam; Sa'd's clan)

sources.quoted: Say: He is Allah, the One!

notes: All dialogue paraphrased from Ibn Ishaq as recalled; confirm, especially 'before Usayd had spoken a word, they could see the change in his face'.
'By evening his clan had' believed: Ibn Ishaq says every man and woman of Banu Abd al-Ashhal accepted Islam by evening; softened to 'tradition says'. Confirm.
The title 'al-muqri'' is from Ibn Ishaq as recalled; confirm the Arabic spelling and transliteration.
Index carry 'the first teacher' kept; the script does not claim he was the first teacher in an absolute sense. A Keeper may wish to confirm the traditional claim.
Pickthall 112:1 quoted; confirm exact wording and punctuation.

Editor pass: Mus'ab's youth and wealthy family are not in the cited Ibn Ishaq passage, so the hook now says 'tradition says' he left a comfortable life, 'young' was dropped from the hook, screen and trapdoor, and the myth item about his family's wealth was replaced with one the script supports (he was sent by the Prophet).
Audit pass: replaced the myth 'won over Usayd by arguing', which repeated day 758's 'persuaded by a long debate' myth, with one on Usayd arriving angry with a spear.
